2.1.4. Biological risk index 
Moist environments lead to mold growth and biological degra- 
dation. Sedlbauer [ 59 ] proposes the isopleth method to estimate 
the risk of biological issues. This method, also cited in relevant Eu- 
ropean and International Standards [ 60 , 61 ], correlates the time pe- 
riod during which speciﬁc T and RH conditions are maintained, to 
various speeds of spore germination and mold growth. Aiming at 
simplifying the model application, Biological Risk Index, BRI, esti- 
mates the percentage of time during which the indoor microcli- 
mate favors biological risks [ 49 ]. 
2.2. Assessment of indoor microclimate variation between pandemic 
and pre-pandemic period 
As previously stated, the monitoring campaign aimed at point- 
ing out possible threatening microclimate conditions, also consid- 
ering that no active climate control measures had been imple- 
mented to regulate air exchange or control indoor environmen- 
tal conditions. However, the pandemic period offered a chance to 
experimentally determine the potential impact of visitors on the 
safe conservation of the artworks. During the pandemic period, in 
fact, the Church went through a period of complete closure (going 
from March 14th to May 18th) and a following period of continu- 
ing opening and closure, depending on the lockdown dispositions. 
Therefore, the analysis of the indoor microclimate includes a 
detailed comparison of the indoor conditions in two conditions, 
one free of visitors, and the other in “classic” condition of people’s 
presence. In particular, four sub-periods have been deﬁned: 
- The baseline period (“BP”), that is, the lockdown period, going 
from 1st April 2020, 0 0:0 0, to 30th April 2020, 23:50; 
- Period “P#1′′ , going from 1st April 2019, 0 0:0 0, to 30th April 
2019, 23:50. 
- Period “P#2′′ , going from 1st July 2019, 0 0:0 0, to 31st July 2019, 
23:50. 
- Period “P#3′′ , going from 1st December 2019, 0 0:0 0, to 31st De- 
cember 2019, 23:50. 
While comparing P#1 and BP would provide speciﬁc results of 
the inﬂuence of visitors’ presence at similar outdoor conditions, 
P#2 and P#3 have been included to add considerations about the 
variation of indoor microclimate in hotter and colder external cli- 
mate. 
3. Results 
3.1. General results of the monitoring period 
The results of the monitoring period pinpoint that the microcli- 
mate inside the Church is variable on an annual basis, with tem- 
perature ranging from about 14 °C to almost 30 °C. Relative hu- 
midity variations range from 35 % to 80 %. However, the daily 
ﬂuctuation is limited, generally remaining within 10 % variation. 
As an example, Fig. 2 shows the temperature, relative humidity, 
and humidity ratio for a 7-day period in January 2020. The ﬁgure 
shows that T is practically homogeneous in the church, with neg- 
ligible differences due to height of measurements (always lower 
than 1 K), or proximity to the main entrance. The humidity ratio, 
illustrated for the same 7-day period in Fig. 2. c, shows on daily ba- 
sis a decrease, in correspondence of the ﬁrst hours of the morning, 
when the main door is open for cleanup; afterwards, the latent 
gains due to visitors and the inﬁltration through windows cause 
an increase of xint , homogeneously in the church. A similar trend is 
found also for the RH values. In the night hours, inﬁltrations from 
outside lead to a reduction of the indoor humidity ratio. 
Table 3 summarizes the average, maximum and minimum val- 
ues of indoor microclimate parameters in the four periods chosen 
for the detailed analysis, compared with some simple statistics of 
Text . Additional results and considerations about the microclimate 
inside the Church are shown in the Supplementary Material. 
3.2. Speciﬁc analysis of the results for assessing inﬂuence of visitors 
on humidity ratio 
For the in-depth analysis on the inﬂuence of visitors on the in- 
door microclimate, the most important parameters are the indoor 
temperature and humidity ratio. These parameters, in fact, are in- 
ﬂuenced by people producing sensible and latent gains, and chang- 
ing ventilation rate. However, indoor temperature variation can be 
altered also by solar gains. In the following, we focus on the vari- 
ation of humidity ratio: in the Supplementary Materials, some ad- 
ditional details about the variation of indoor temperature can be 
found. 
To strengthen the soundness of the results about the inﬂuence 
of visitors, an error analysis has been also carried out. For temper- 
ature analysis, the accuracy of the sensors has been set to quantify 
the 95 %-conﬁdence interval. As the nameplate data of the sensors 
relate to error in relative humidity measurements, a Monte Carlo 
analysis has been applied to estimate the error on humidity ra- 
tio, starting from rough data of temperature and relative humidity. 
This methodology is in fact widely used in all those cases where 
non-linearities are present, impeding the use of classic error prop- 
agation analysis [ 62 ]. 
Fig. 3 represents the diurnal path of indoor humidity ratio for 
the four reference periods. The diurnal variation of xint is more ev- 
ident in the three pre-pandemic periods, than in BP.

3.3. Estimation of the risk indicators 
The previous analyses have discussed the inﬂuence of people 
presence to indoor microclimate, providing only preliminary indi- 
cations about possible critical conditions reached inside. The actual 
effects of the indoor microclimate on the frescoes are estimated 
through the speciﬁc indices’ calculation. Table 4 provides the val- 
ues of the four indicators deﬁned in Section 3.1 for the four peri- 
ods: the unacceptable values are written in bold. 
As previously stated, the estimation of PI has been reported for 
sake of completeness, as this indicator is used in other works on 
museums and worship places. However, as there is not a general 
consensus on the threshold limits, we have not considered the low 
values of this indicator as a signal of preservation risk for artworks.

microclimate control systems, a monitoring campaign was carried 
out, assessing the level of risk posed by indoor climate, and pro- 
viding a basis for understanding the impact of environmental fac- 
tors on artwork conservation. Data were collected over a period of 
655 days, with a 10-min acquisition. A low-cost monitoring sys- 
tem comprising a mini-PC and wireless digital sensors (Si7021A20 
wireless digital sensors from Silicon LabsTM ) was employed, moni- 
toring T and RH. Each sensor was individually calibrated before the 
monitoring campaign. The characteristics of the employed sensors 
are the following: 
• T : accuracy ± 0.4 K in the range −10 ÷85 °C, 
• RH: accuracy ± 3 % in the range 0 ÷80 %; accuracy ± 5 % in the 
range 80 ÷100 %. 
Table 2 summarizes the position and orientation of the sensors, 
together with their IDs. Some additional details about the sensors 
and their position in the Church, including a plan of the Church 
ﬂoor, can be found in the Supplementary Material. 
During the study, outdoor climate data were obtained from a 
meteorological station situated near the building. 
As previously mentioned, this monitoring campaign took place 
within a period lasting almost two years, from September 2018 to 
July 2020. During the ﬁrst few months of the monitoring campaign, 
some technical issues occurred, which resulted in the dataset not 
always being complete. For this reason, the data used in this arti- 
cle starts from May 2019, as from this date onwards, there are no 
more ’gaps’ in the data. The monitoring campaign then ended in 
July 2020. Thus, in this time frame, two distinct periods can be 
identiﬁed, differing from presence of people and rate of air ex- 
change: 
• a "regular" period (May 2019 - February 2020), during which 
the church was open during daytime. Beyond tourists’ visit- 
ing, various activities were conducted (e.g., masses, music re- 
hearsals, cleanup). Tourist access to the premises was capped 
and scheduled for up to 200 visitors; the visiting hours were 
regulated from 7:30 to 20:15 in winter, and from 9:00 to 14:30 
in summer. Air exchange during visitor access was not actively 
controlled. Doors were kept open during daytime for liturgical 
activities and to allow tourists to visit the church and its fres- 
coes, further inﬂuencing indoor T and RH. Fresh air ingress oc- 
curred also through door openings during cleaning operations. 
Additionally, some windows remained permanently open due 
to accessibility constraints; 
• the pandemic period, starting March 2020, during which the 
church was closed, with neither the inﬂuence of internal gains 
nor increased ventilation rate due to door openings on indoor 
microclimate. A few windows still remained open, due to ac- 
cessibility constraints. 
2. Methodology 
2.1. Analysis of the data for artwork preservation 
Scientiﬁc literature provides different methods for assessing 
whether indoor microclimate conditions are responsible for art- 
works’ degradation. Some methods, gathered under the umbrella 
of the “microclimate methodology”, state that only maintaining 
speciﬁc temperature and humidity values, or minimizing the de- 
viations from them to the utmost, ensures preservation. Some oth- 
ers, instead, model the mechanisms involved in degradation, thus 
estimating the actual level of risk, and can be gathered under the 
umbrella of the “risk-assessment methodology”. The two method- 
ologies are not in conﬂict, as each of them examines only a portion 
of the artworks’ degradation problem, which instead encompasses 
many different interconnected aspects. Therefore, a more compre- 
hensive and cohesive overview is obtained using both methodolo- 
gies [ 49 ]. 
Literature also provides speciﬁc indicators to check the preser- 
vation of artworks. In this research, we have considered the fol- 
lowing: 
• Performance Index, PI, relating to microclimate threshold set- 
points (microclimate methodology). 
• Daily Span Index, DSI, relating to maximum values of microcli- 
mate span (microclimate methodology). 
• Equivalent Lifetime Multiplier, ELM, assessing the chemical risk 
of damage (risk-assessment methodology) 
• Biological Risk Index, BRI, assessing the biological risk of dam- 
age (risk-assessment methodology). 
In the following Sections, the four indicators are discussed. 
2.1.1. Performance index 
This indicator, PI, ﬁrst deﬁned by [ 50 ], represents the percent- 
age of time during which the T and RH remain within the optimal 
range, which depends on the typology of artwork. As it is easy to 
assess and understand, this indicator is one of the most employed 
in literature (see, for example, [ 33 , 50 ]). However, identifying estab- 
lished and unique microclimate limit values to avoid risks is diﬃ- 
cult. A wide number of standards and guidelines (e.g., [ 11 , 51–53 ]), 
in fact, suggest different ranges of T and RH for the same type of 
artwork. 
In this work, UNI 10829:1999 [ 54 ] provides the set conditions 
for frescoes: T in 10–24 °C range, RH in 55–65 % range. 
2.1.2. Daily span index 
Daily microclimate variation occurs always in environments 
where HVAC system is intermittently operated (e.g., heating 
switched off at night). Thomson [ 2 ] relates those daily variation 
to daily “fatigue” cycles of expansion and contraction, accelerating 
degradation. First deﬁned in [ 55 ], the daily span index, DSI, rep- 
resents the percentage of days during which the measured daily 
variations in T and RH do not exceed the suggested range. UNI 
10829:1999 [ 54 ] provides suggested maximum daily span for T and 
RH (2 K and 8 %, respectively). 
2.1.3. Equivalent lifetime multiplier index 
This indicator is related to all those chemical mechanisms 
involved in artworks degradation, as discoloration or chromatic 
changes. Michalski [ 56 ] models the risks associated with those 
mechanisms by deﬁning an equivalent lifetime multiplier, ELM, 
which represents an estimation of how much the time period be- 
tween two necessary cycles of restoration of the artwork is altered 
by internal microclimate. Thus, a value of ELM signiﬁcantly lower 
than 1 indicates an accelerated chemical degradation. The model 
has been reﬁned by [ 57 , 58 ].

a b s t r a c t 
In churches, especially those without mechanical climate control systems, indoor temperature and relative 
humidity can ﬂuctuate signiﬁcantly throughout the day and year, posing potential risks to the preser- 
vation of artworks such as frescoes and wooden objects. The intermittent presence of people in these 
environments can exacerbate the problem, as their sensible and latent heat contributions amplify mi- 
croclimate ﬂuctuations. However, the actual impact of people on the indoor microclimate and artwork 
degradation is challenging to estimate due to the diﬃculty of collecting data during periods of contin- 
uous absence. In this paper, we monitored indoor environmental parameters inside the Santos Juanes 
Church, a temple of historical value in Valencia, Spain, from 2019 to 2020. This allowed us to assess 
the actual impact of visitors on the indoor microclimate through a comparative analysis of data from a 
"typical" period of use and data from the COVID-19 lockdown, when the church was closed. The results 
indicate that the effects of indoor activities on the microclimate are limited, not causing speciﬁc dam- 
age related to daily ﬂuctuations. However, the estimation of damage risk indicators shows that indoor 
conditions during the summer, inﬂuenced by high outdoor temperatures and solar radiation, are not ad- 
equate for proper preservation. This issue, potentially common to many other churches in hot climates, 
can be addressed with increased night ventilation. This simple solution avoids the use of complex me- 
chanical systems, which increase carbon emissions and are not recommended in the context of historical 
buildings.

1. Introduction 
1.1. Context and state of the art 
Historic buildings, such as churches or palaces, are often build- 
ings of architectural interest, containing themselves artworks of 
cultural signiﬁcance. Indoor microclimate is universally recognized 
as one of the main factors hampering the integrity of artworks 
[ 1–3 ], together with light, gaseous pollutants, dust, and micro- 
bial colonies. Each parameter causes speciﬁc damage to artworks, 
threatening their integrity. As an example, ultraviolet radiation 
may cause photochemical phenomena, and pollutants may cause 
oxidation and catalysis. Dry temperature (T) and relative humidity 
(RH) are responsible for a variety of deterioration processes, such 
as fungi and mold growth and varnish deterioration [ 4 , 5 ]. Abrupt 
changes in microclimate are dangerous as well, causing thermal

[ 6 ]. Moreover, interactions among degradation factors can further 
exacerbate all those effects. As an example, unsuitable values of 
both T and RH increases the effects of swelling-shrinking cycles. A 
relevant number of pieces of research have correlated inadequate 
microclimate conditions to various degradation phenomena [ 1 , 3 , 7–
10 ]. Scholars [ 1 , 3 ] also seek for T and RH setpoints for optimal art- 
work preservation. Some technical standards (e.g., [ 11 , 12 ]) propose 
speciﬁc appropriate ranges of ﬂuctuations for microclimate to be 
maintained. Heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) sys- 
tems are often used to maintain stable indoor conditions: those 
systems are often necessary in case of strict conservation require- 
ments of the artworks. At the same time, using HVAC systems 
poses questions due to their high purchase and energy costs and 
environmental emissions. As stated in [ 13 ], the continuous oper- 
ation of air conditioning in those places would be too expensive 
for the institutions managing the buildings. Besides, if also contin- 
uously operating, HVAC systems are often set to meet human ther-

Regarding the principal issues for artworks preservation, the 
performed analyses have shown that too high temperatures in 
summer can increase risks for chemical degradation, with expected 
lifetime of the frescoes halved. In winter, instead, the thermo- 
physical properties of the church envelope help in maintaining 
favorable microclimate conditions, as the temperature inside the 
zone is kept stable at a value closer to the most suitable range 
( ∼15 −20◦C), with a relative humidity around 50 %. Issues re- 
lated to high temperatures are not so frequently identiﬁed in lit- 
erature. In literature, similar problems have been identiﬁed in 
[ 27 , 41 ], which in fact refer to churches in the Mediterranean cli- 
mate (Naples in Italy, and Malta, respectively). Generally speaking, 
scholars have often identiﬁed problems related to low indoor tem- 
peratures and high relative humidity in winter, thus leading to risk 
of mold growth: some examples can be found in [ 24 , 29 , 39 , 63 ]. It 
should be noted that, however, a larger volume of papers in lit- 
erature concerns churches in cold climates, compared to those in 
warmer and Mediterranean climates. 
4.2. Night cooling as a proposal for reducing high indoor temperature 
in cooling season 
The current microclimate inside the Church is unacceptable for 
ensuring artworks’ preservation only in the warm period. However, 
as discussed in other pieces of research (e.g., [ 41 ]), installation 
of complete HVAC systems, including air handling units or heat- 
ing/cooling terminal units, is usually not recommended, or even 
forbidden to preserve the historic value of the building itself. Be- 
sides, in the case of Santos Juanes Church, the system would work 
only in a limited period of the year, as the indoor conditions are 
acceptable in the winter and spring. Therefore, the purchasing and 
maintenance costs of a complete HVAC system may also represent 
an obstacle. Besides, the HVAC system installation is generally con- 
sidered as an “invasive” solution, leading to compromising the in- 
trinsic historical, aesthetic, and architectural values of the building. 
A good compromise for improving microclimate in summer sea- 
son without a too large investment need could be night-cooling, 
also known as free-cooling, or night ventilation [ 64 ]: this is a pas- 
sive cooling technique consisting in an increased air ventilation 
ratio at nighttime, when outdoor air is cooler than inside. This 
helps in the cooling of the indoor air and building envelope, slow- 
ing down the rise of the indoor air temperature during daytime. 
According to the authors’ best knowledge, this solution, although 
simple, is rarely proposed for microclimate improvement. In [ 65 ], 
a similar solution, named “adaptive ventilation” by the authors, is 
proposed as a way to reduce the indoor humidity ratio: when x 
inside is higher than that outside, a fan is switched on to increase 
air change rate. In the present paper, instead, increased rate of air 
change is proposed to lower Tint . 
To verify the suitability of this solution, the following Fig. 6. a 
compares the external temperature and the indoor temperature in 
July 2019, for different hours. In the ﬁgure, the black dotted line 
represents the threshold limit for the “ideal” convenience of this 
strategy: points at the left of this line represent external conditions 
favorable for the cooling of the building. Increasing ventilation rate 
if the external temperature lies at the right-bottom corner of the 
ﬁgure, instead, does not provide beneﬁts (outdoor temperature is 
higher than inside), so it should be avoided. 
Fig. 6. a shows that the opening of doors and windows (or the 
installation of a mechanical ventilation system) is generally not 
recommended if implemented in the ﬁrst hours of the evening 
(e.g., before 21:00), as the average external temperature is sim- 
ilar, or even higher, to the indoor temperature. On the contrary, 
increasing ventilation rates during nights up to the ﬁrst hours of 
the morning (i.e., from midnight to 8:00) could help in the re- 
duction of indoor temperature, therefore reducing chemical risks 
for the artworks. Fig. 6. b shows that, during the same hours, the 
xext can ﬂuctuate within a relatively wide range of approximately 
12–20 g/kg. No clear trend is observed based on the time of day. 
Therefore, by appropriately selecting the ventilation rate, it is pos- 
sible to slightly reduce the internal temperature without signiﬁ- 
cantly altering the relative humidity, thus avoiding drastic changes 
in the microclimate. This result is consistent with the discussion 
in Michalski’s paper [ 42 ], which describes night cooling as one of 
the most effective means of cooling buildings, provided it does not 
cause an undesirable increase in internal relative humidity. 
It is important to note that the effective convenience of this 
technique can be assessed only by means of a complete dynamic 
simulation of the building, as the effective night-time airﬂow rate, 
the building shape and construction inﬂuence the effectiveness of 
night ventilation similarly to the indoor-outdoor temperature dif-

The indoor values of T and RH do not represent a mechanical or 
biological danger for the artworks, as the values of BRI and DSI are 
acceptable. Chemical risk is, instead, present. The value of ELM is 
below 0.5 in P#2, that is, the summer month used as reference. 
Fig. 5 shows the indoor temperature and relative humidity values 
for the four periods. In the ﬁgure, the chemical risks are repre- 
sented as LM isolines: in other words, the ’0.5’ line represents all 
the pairs of Tint and RHint halving the life of the fresco. The indoor 
values referring to BP, P#1 and P#3 are all in proximity of the ’1’ 
curve, meaning that the microclimate does not represent a risk for 
the artwork. Conversely, values of indoor temperature are too high 
in P#2 (July 2019): all the markers lie beyond the ’0.5’ line. 
Although the results presented in the previous paragraph con- 
ﬁrm that visitors do have an impact on indoor microclimate, the 
risk indicators show that this does not pose a real risk to artwork 
preservation: conservation risks are primarily linked to the indoor 
high temperatures reached in summer. 
4. Discussion and implications on indoor microclimate 
4.1. Comparison of the results with previous studies 
Scientiﬁc literature highlights that daily variation of T and RH
is one of the main risks for preservation, as discussed, for exam- 
ple, in [ 25 ] (daily RH variation up to 40 %), [ 26 ] (peaks of T up to 
10 K due to direct solar radiation on artworks), and [ 33 ] (where 
RH daily ﬂuctuations up to 30 % are found, especially in proximity 
to the main door, while on the opposite side, RH is more stable). 
Our analysis, however, shows that there is only a limited risk for 
artworks due to daily microclimate variation. Inﬁltration through 
the windows causes a limited variation in the indoor values of 
temperature and humidity ratio. During the pandemic period, in 
fact, the daily ﬂuctuations of humidity ratio have been signiﬁcantly 
lower than the ones observed in the other three periods, due to 
the low inﬁltration rate when windows are not completely open. 
The higher ﬂuctuations in the other three pre-pandemic periods 
are due to both the presence of people (increasing vapor content 
during the ﬁrst part of the day), and the opening of the main doors 
(occurring generally in the morning for cleaning operation, lower- 
ing the humidity ratio). However, DSI is higher than 0.85 in all pe- 
riods except for December, where this indicator is around 0.75 any- 
way. Besides, the thermal inertia of the Church is high, this feature 
limiting daily microclimate variability. The relatively low variation 
in speciﬁc humidity, even when a large number of people is ex- 
pected to be inside, is also a consequence of the large volume.

The presence of people inside places of worship or museums is 
considered an additional constraint for all professionals who must 
design and properly operate an HVAC system. However, visitors in- 
ﬂuence the microclimate, both for their internal heat and vapor 
gains, and for the alteration of air changes and mixing ratio with 
outdoor air due to actively opening and closing doors. Both factors 
inﬂuence the energy balance of the indoor environment, and can 
then either threaten or help (depending on the other terms of the 
energy balance) the maintenance of the most suitable indoor con- 
ditions for artworks, particularly in buildings without HVAC sys- 
tems. Connections among visitors’ presence, indoor microclimate 
ﬂuctuations, and artwork preservation are less explored. Going into 
detail, the following considerations can be formulated: 
• The analysis of the actual inﬂuence of people to microclimate 
is typically carried out by comparison of indoor microclimate 
values during reference days with and without people inside 
churches. However, the comparison of single days does not en- 
sure that effects of daily microclimate ﬂuctuations are only 
caused by individuals’ presence. Additional reasons, not dealing 
with people presence, may not be detected in such temporally 
limited analyses. Thus, it is important to compare prolongated 
periods of absence and presence of people, a condition that is 
not easy to realize in buildings that are tourist attractions; 
• The classic approach to assess the inﬂuence of microclimate on 
degradation is the comparison of indoor microclimate with sug- 
gested values by guidelines, and/or the calculation of statistical 
indicators, as distribution of temperature and relative humidity 
daily ﬂuctuations: this approach, however, gives only a prelim- 
inary glance at possible preservation problems, which can be 
identiﬁed by means of more detailed methodologies; 
• To identify preliminary solutions to improve indoor microcli- 
mate, keeping it more adequate for artwork preservation, the 
classic approach is the dynamic simulation of the building sys- 
tem and the comparison of different retroﬁt strategies, involv- 
ing either (or both) passive and active solutions. Although this 
methodology is by far more precise, some preliminary solutions 
can be identiﬁed also by an in-depth analysis of the gathered 
data during monitoring campaigns. After the preliminary iden- 
tiﬁcation of those solutions, a more detailed analysis can be 
then performed to determine the real advantages of the pro- 
posed strategies. 
1.3. Aim of the research 
In this context, this research offers a contribution to scientiﬁc 
literature through the analysis of indoor microclimate in the Santos 
Juanes Church in València, Spain. This church is an historic build- 
ing, the internal walls of which are heavily decorated with fres- 
coes. Beyond being a tourist attraction, it is also used for Chris- 
tian celebrations, and for rehearsals of choir and orchestra. With 
the aim of checking if indoor microclimate is adequate for frescoes 
preservation, a monitoring campaign started in 2018, scheduled to 
ﬁnish in 2020. The pandemic period in 2020 offered the oppor- 
tunity to monitor the indoor microclimate conditions without the 
inﬂuence of people for an extended period, not limited to the few 
hours of individuals’ absence at night. In this paper, indoor climate 
ﬂuctuations in the pandemic period are compared to ﬂuctuations 
in the previous year, thus allowing to evidence of the actual inﬂu- 
ence of people in indoor microclimate. Data from monitoring cam- 
paign are also used with the aim of identifying issues for artwork 
integrity and seeking preliminary solutions to be implemented. 
1.4. The Santos Juanes Church in Valencia 
In this piece of research, we analyze the data of a monitoring 
campaign carried out in the Santos Juanes Church, in the city of 
Fig. 1. Original photograph of the current painting in the central nave vault in the 
south area. 
Valencia. According to Köppen classiﬁcation [ 43 ], Valencian area 
stands between Mediterranean “Csa ” climate, and semi-arid “Bsh ”
climate, with particularly hot summers and mild winters. This con- 
sideration is crucial for analyzing all the results found within the 
speciﬁc context of the city’s external climate, and comparing them 
with those in the literature pertaining to similar external climate 
environments. 
The Church of Santos Juanes (Real Parroquia de los Santos 
Juanes) in Valencia was originally built in 1240 as a mosque, and 
has undergone a series of alterations over the centuries due to 
ﬁres, resulting in a complex architectural assemblage. The most re- 
cent reconstruction occurred in the 17th and 18th centuries, dur- 
ing which the temple was transformed in an outstanding example 
of the Valencian Baroque style, concealing its original Gothic style 
and inﬂuenced by Italian artists and local cultural elite [ 44 ]. De- 
spite the implementation of several subsequent restoration effort s, 
including one following a ﬁre during the Spanish Civil War in 1936, 
the church required constant interventions to maintain its favor- 
able state [ 45 ]. Since 2004, experimental investigations have been 
conducted on a portion of the vault, which have presented signif- 
icant technical challenges [ 46 ], necessitating the development of 
speciﬁc methodologies for cleaning and consolidation, also using 
3D models and digital techniques [ 47 , 48 ]. 
The Santos Juanes Church is home to a variety of artistic mas- 
terpieces, including groups of paintings, sculptures, and decora- 
tive elements. Of particular note are the ornate stuccoes adorning 
the central nave, the intricate paintings that grace the ovals be- 
tween arches and entablature, the vibrant murals that adorn the 
side chapels, and the poignant murals that adorn the Communion 
Chapel. However, the true crown jewel of the Church’s heritage is 
undoubtedly the magniﬁcent ceiling frescoes created by Antonio 
Palomino. Palomino, a distinguished 17th-century Spanish painter, 
depicted the Celestial Glory using techniques of perspective and 
quadrature [ 47 , 48 ]. The iconographic program of the vault includes 
the twelve apostles and their respective allegories, as well as God 
the Father and the Holy Spirit, who are depicted surrounded by a 
multitude of heavenly choirs, saints, and angels (see Fig. 1 ) [ 47 , 48 ]. 
Given the artistic relevance of Palomino’s frescoes, in this paper we 
will focus on the preservation of them. 
The church is characterized by thick masonry walls and wooden 
single-glazed windows, with a total volume of about 14,500 m3 
and an orientation W-E (main entrance on west side, apse on east 
side). There is no ﬁxed heating or air conditioning system. Gas 
stoves are occasionally employed in the winter and simple fans 
in the summer. Furthermore, doors are kept open during daytime, 
due to liturgical activities and historical interest of the building, to 
give tourists the possibility of visiting the church and the frescoes 
on the walls. No speciﬁc ventilation strategy and climate control 
measures had been implemented at the time. 
No preventive conservation actions have been carried out in the 
church in past years, despite their potential beneﬁts in preserving 
the artworks and preventing future damage. Given the absence of

mal comfort requirements, barely considering the issues related to 
artwork preservation. 
As highlighted by technical standard EN 15757 [ 14 ], even chang- 
ing the indoor conditions may potentially compromise the con- 
servation of collections that have already been adapted to speciﬁc 
conditions. In the case of buildings without HVAC system, in fact, 
artworks become “adapted” to the indoor free-ﬂoating temperature 
and relative humidity, undergoing deterioration in case of microcli- 
mate sudden variation (e.g., if an HVAC system is ﬁnally installed). 
For instance, an artwork that has been in a humid environment 
may undergo mechanical deformations if suddenly moved to a dry 
climate, with materials like wood, paper, or paint quickly reacting 
to the new conditions. In this regard, Silva et al. [ 15 ] note that, af- 
ter being exposed to certain climate conditions, artworks can expe- 
rience long-lasting deformation and lose their ability to “adapt” to 
other new climate conditions without damage. Such abrupt shifts 
do not allow for gradual adaptation (sometimes known as “stress 
relaxation” [ 16 ]), potentially causing irreversible damage. EN 15757 
[ 14 ], in particular, gives emphasis to the role of RH as leading dam- 
aging mechanism, and deﬁnes RH setpoints using an annual mean 
and a 30-day central moving average (CMA30): this approach at- 
tempts to reconcile the conﬂicting demands of historic building 
preservation and occupant comfort. The target RH values change 
throughout the year, implying intrinsic sustainability, requiring less 
energy to reach setpoints closer to the outdoor climate. In the ab- 
sence of historical data, it is recommended that a minimum mon- 
itoring period of 13 months be employed in order to calculate the 
CMA30. In the absence of RH records, ﬂuctuations up to 10 % are 
required [ 14 ]. Prior to any assessment of the chemical-mechanical 
properties of the artwork, it is essential to verify the process will 
not cause damage. Should the necessity arise, the upper and lower 
limits of the RH range may be adjusted. 
Historic buildings, and churches in particular, are usually not 
equipped with HVAC systems, and only a limited number of them 
use heating generators (e.g., [ 17 ]) or cooling generators (e.g., [ 18 ]), 
depending on the external climate. Furthermore, their envelopes 
are usually characterized by high inertia walls and a limited glazed 
area. Depending on the daily and seasonal ﬂuctuations, these 
buildings may represent ideal or harmful environments. Collecting 
and analyzing accurate data help conservators to assess the state 
of conservation of collections. 
The scientiﬁc state of the art has been analyzed on this topic, 
by querying SCOPUS database using the keywords {“Church”, “Mi- 
croclimate”}. The reading of abstracts has reﬁned the results, ex- 
cluding papers dealing with simulation tools (e.g., [ 13 , 19 , 20 ]) and 
maintaining only papers showing results of monitoring campaigns 
in churches. Finally, 22 articles (see Table 1 ) have been selected 
and read. 
In accordance with guidelines and standards (e.g. [ 11 ]), precise 
thermo-hygrometric data should be recorded on a short-scale spa- 
tial granularity, even if in some cases a compromise between accu- 
racy of data and costs sustainability is sought. That compromise is 
conﬁrmed by the literature, where duration and number of probes 
appear to be extremely variable. As an example, some monitoring 
campaigns lasted for a few weeks (e.g., [ 21 , 22 ]), some months (e.g., 
[ 18 , 22–24 ]), or more than one year (e.g., [ 17 , 25–27 ]), with a single 
case reporting a 6-year measurement [ 28 ]. Recording data setting 
ranges from 5 min (e.g., [ 27 ]) up to 1 hour (e.g., [ 17 ]). Because of 
their importance in artwork deterioration process, T and RH are 
always measured parameters; sometimes wall surface temperature 
(e.g., [ 29 ]), humidity ratio x (e.g., [ 30 ]) and air velocity (e.g., [ 25 ]) 
are measured as well. In a single case [ 31 ], a thermographic cam- 
era is used for measurements of surface temperature. The number 
of measurement points varies, ranging from only one probe [ 32 ] to 
more than 20 sensors [ 22 ]. Literature was analyzed also to under- 
stand how the monitored data were used by scholars, and for what 
purpose. Typically, scholars look for spatial gradients and microcli- 
mate daily variation (e.g., [ 15 , 22 ]), compare indoor climatic param- 
eters with reference values for artwork preservation (e.g., [ 21 , 29 ]), 
check the inﬂuence of thermal mass on the correlation between 
outside and inside climate (e.g., [ 25 , 28 ]). The two most applied 
methodologies for detecting possible risks for artworks are: (1) the 
comparison of indoor T and RH values with recommended values 
from technical standards (e.g., [ 21 , 33 ]), and (2) the statistical anal- 
ysis of the spatial and daily variations of those parameters (e.g., 
[ 15 , 18 , 21 ]). 
Speciﬁc research on the inﬂuence of visitors on indoor micro- 
climate has received only a limited attention. In particular, Varas- 
Muriel et al. [ 6 ] compares the microclimate parameters recorded 
inside the San Juan Bautista Church when church is full (e.g., dur- 
ing Christmas or special rites) and when individuals’ presence is 
sporadic. Metals et al. [ 24 ] also use a similar approach, confronting 
the effects on spatial variation of microclimate due to visitors’ 
number. Finally, Huerto-Cardenas et al. [ 33 ] analyze the inﬂuence 
of visitors’ presence on indoor microclimate: in their paper, some 
statistical indicators have been evaluated, pointing out that a lim- 
ited number of visitors inside the Church reduces the daily ﬂuctu- 
ations of T and RH. 
Table 1 summarizes the main features of the literature dealing 
with monitoring campaigns in churches. 
1.2. Discussion on the literature review 
The literature review has pointed out a strong interest in mi- 
croclimate measurement in churches, focusing on optimal temper- 
ature and humidity conditions to avoid degradation of the art- 
works. Some studies also explore balancing visitor comfort with 
the preservation needs of artworks and the building (e.g., [ 42 ]).

a drastic decrease in T , also related to RH variation, which would 
increase risks related to daily ﬂuctuations. This aspect will be ob- 
ject of future research, with the speciﬁc aim of optimizing ventila- 
tion rate to “passively” reduce overheating in the Church, avoiding 
abrupt RH variation. 
5. Conclusions 
The present paper has examined data collected in the Santos 
Juanes Church, in a prolonged period including lockdown in April 
2020. Data of temperature and relative humidity were used to seek 
the impact of visitors in changing indoor microclimate conditions 
and potentially hamper artworks’ preservation. On this regard, the 
following conclusions can be drawn: 
• the comparative analysis of data during and previous lockdown 
during COVID-19 pandemic does not give indication of possible 
risk to be directly or indirectly correlated to individuals’ pres- 
ence. Even if daily microclimate ﬂuctuations (especially those of 
humidity ratio) are more evident in pre-pandemic period, they 
are not suﬃcient to cause damage. 
• the estimation of speciﬁc artwork risk assessment indicators 
highlights that chemical risk is present in summer period. This 
is due to the high outside temperatures, direct solar radiation 
on the church envelope, and lack of a cooling system. This 
problem is not commonly found in literature, which has been 
more focused on churches located in colder climates. How- 
ever, it can represent a widespread problem in many similar 
churches located in hotter climates. Thus, those results argue 
for more research activities on the indoor microclimate in hot 
and semi-arid climates. 
• the gathered data hint that a possible solution for the summer 
overheating inside the church can be an increase ventilation 
during nights, where outdoor temperature is lower than that 
inside. This preliminary solution needs, of course, a higher level 
of detail, to check how the building geometry and materials 
would inﬂuence the temperature decrease, and simultaneously 
avoid risk of too wide daily temperature ﬂuctuations. In any 
case, it represents an alternative solution to those involving the 
installation of HVAC systems, which can be questioned in his- 
torical building context. At the same time, considering current 
policies aimed at the reduction of energy requirements, the use 
of those devices would result in energy consumptions, previ- 
ously absent. Night ventilation, instead, may ensure preserva- 
tion of the artworks with a negligible effect on energy con- 
sumption and related carbon emissions. 
Further work will focus on modeling night ventilation and 
checking the actual potential of this strategy in reducing indoor 
temperature in summer.
